summary: Ages 5–6 (Reception/Year 1) rote counting to (and across) 100: reciting the number-word sequence fluently by ones — forwards and backwards, beginning from 0, 1, or any given number. The aim is to build a stable, repeatable ordered list of number words that object counting, place value and skip counting later run on, while distinguishing reciting the sequence from counting objects. Target the two predictable break points: the irregular teens (eleven, twelve, thirteen — not 'oneteen') and the decade boundaries (…28, 29 → 30; …39 → 40). Backward counting and starting mid-sequence are harder than forward-from-one and must be practised explicitly. A hundred square exposes the repeating 0–9 ones pattern so counting becomes prediction, not pure memory.
misconceptions: Decade-boundary stalls: '…28, 29, twenty-ten' or jumping to the wrong decade — the ones-cycle-to-next-ten transition isn't secured.
Irregular teens: 'eleventeen', or mapping teen words to the wrong quantity; hearing 'thirteen' as 30.
Counting forward from one but not backward or from a mid-point — the sequence is stored as a single forward chant.
Confusing rote reciting with meaningful counting — chanting numbers with nothing attached and assuming that IS counting.

activities.title: Predict across the decade boundary on a hundred square
steps: Point to a chosen starting cell on a hundred square (e.g. 67) and count on aloud, moving a pointer or marker cell by cell: '68, 69…'
As you approach a decade boundary, pause and predict the next number BEFORE saying it ('after 69 comes…?') and check whether the tens goes up by one ten (to 70) rather than inventing 'sixty-ten'.
Trace down a single column and say the numbers aloud to notice the ones digit stays the same while the tens digit climbs.
Repeat for the rehearsed seams: 28, 29, 30 and 38, 39, 40, until each bridge is automatic.
Then run the marker the other way to count backward across a boundary (e.g. 41, 40, 39…).
activities.insight: 100 numbers are not 100 separate things to memorise: the ones digits cycle through 0–9 again and again (on a 1–100 square each row runs from 1 to 10, e.g. 31–40; on a 0–99 square from 0 to 9, e.g. 40–49). So once you know the repeating ones pattern, the decade words and the irregular teens, and can cross cleanly into the next ten, most of the sequence becomes predictable.

activities.title: Start anywhere and keep going
steps: On being given a starting number (e.g. 'start at 23'), begin the count there and continue forward WITHOUT going back to 1 first.
Practise entering the sequence from many different points — a visible number track or hundred square can mark where to begin.
Count on and across 100 to see the sequence continues (what comes after 100?), consistent with the 'to and across 100' standard.

Count backward from a given number: begin with short runs (e.g. 5 down to 0, then 15 down to 0) as scaffolds, then build up to 20 down to 0 without gaps, and on towards the full target of counting back from any given number up to 100 (e.g. 100 down to 90, 73 down to 60), including across decade boundaries. Use a number line or hundred square and, if helpful, a physical step-down for each number.
activities.insight: The number-word list should be accessible from any point and in both directions, not only as a single forward chant started at one.

activities.title: Daily rhythmic oral counting and take-turns buddy counting
steps: Count aloud daily in short, rhythmic bursts — chants, songs or choral counting with the class or an adult.
Take turns with a partner (or a count-with-me buddy): you say one number, they say the next, alternating up the sequence.
When the buddy deliberately stumbles at a decade boundary ('…29… twenty-ten?'), catch and correct it.
Rehearse the irregular teens as a named stretch (eleven, twelve, thirteen…) and check you are not hearing 'thirteen' as 30.
activities.insight: The oral number sequence is built little and often, as sound and rhythm; taking turns and fixing a buddy's stumble makes the learner produce and monitor the sequence rather than just hear it.

activities.title: Fill the gap and fix the sequence (retrieval practice)
steps: Fill in a missing number in a sequence (e.g. _, 29, _) and say what comes after 29 (30) and what comes just before 60 (59).
Put jumbled number cards back into order.
Count back a set number of steps from a given start.
Spot and fix a recite that has an omitted or doubled number (…14, 15, 17…).
activities.insight: Secure rote counting means you can enter, continue, reverse and repair the sequence — not only chant it from the start.

checkQuestion: Count out loud from 1, as far as you can, up to 100. Then I'll stop you and give a new place to start: begin at 23 and keep going. Last, count backwards from 20 down to 0. (Watch the decade boundaries, whether they can start mid-sequence, and whether backward counting holds.)
checkAnswer: Recites 1–100 in order with no omissions or repeats, crosses each decade boundary cleanly (…29, 30…; …49, 50…), resumes forward from 23 without restarting at 1, and counts back 20→0 without gaps.
